# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 7. Triangulation
md(r"""
---
## 7. Triangulation: do the verbatims and the study agree?

Each requirement area is matched to its feedback topics (by keyword on the VFC topic name) and its study attributes
(by name). An area is **strong evidence** when both sources point the same way, and **conflicting** when one says
it's a problem and the other says it's fine. The mapping is hand-made and transparent. Edit `AREAS` to change it.
""")

code(r"""
AREAS = {
    # area: (regex on feedback topic, list of US study attributes)
    "Operating concept / HMI": (r"operating concept|touch ?screen|instrument cluster|body equipment, overall|operation",
                                ["Intuitiveness of controls", "Placement/ ease of reading and using controls",
                                 "Overall driver-vehicle interaction (HMI)", "Menu structure of infotainment system",
                                 "Ease of reading and using screen interface"]),
    "Smartphone integration": (r"apple carplay|android|smartphone|bluetooth|wireless charg|phone",
                               ["Bluetooth/ smartphone pairing", "Mirroring of smartphone content on vehicle display",
                                "Place for phone", "Phone charging"]),
    "Connected services & app": (r"connecteddrive|app\b|my bmw|remote|digital key|wi-?fi|hotspot|navigation",
                                 ["Vehicle's Mobile App", "WiFi hotspot in vehicle", "If applicable: Navigation system"]),
    "Voice control": (r"voice|speech|intelligent personal assistant",
                      ["Performance of voice recognition"]),
    "Climate controls": (r"climat|heating|air condition|ventilat",
                         ["Operation of heater/ AC controls", "Overall performance of climate control system"]),
    "Seats & comfort": (r"seat|interior comfort",
                        ["Overall comfort of the seats", "Comfort of front seat", "Comfort of 2nd row seat",
                         "Driver seat adjustability"]),
    "Storage & cargo": (r"storage|luggage|trunk|stowage|cup ?holder",
                        ["Interior storage", "Cargo capacity/usefulness", "Ease of loading/unloading cargo",
                         "Trunk lid/ tailgate and liftgate operations", "Cupholders"]),
    "Range & charging (EV)": (r"electric range|charg(e|ing) high|public charging|charging|high-voltage",
                              ["Gas or electric mileage (fuel economy)", "Overall environmental friendliness"]),
    "Driver assistance": (r"assist|cruise control|parking|lane|camera",
                          ["Overall driver assist features", "Adaptive driving assists (lane keeping, cruise, braking)",
                           "Safety monitoring features (blid spot warning, lane departure warning, etc)"]),
    "Start-stop & drivetrain feel": (r"start-stop|msa|drivetrain|transmission",
                                     ["Overall power and pickup", "Smoothness of transmission", "Acceleration from stop"]),
    "Ride & handling": (r"handling|riding|driving dynamics|chassis|steering|braking",
                        ["Riding comfort", "Handling/Maneuverability", "Overall driving performance", "Braking"]),
    "Exterior design": (r"exterior design|^exterior$|lights?\b|wheel",
                        ["Overall exterior styling", "Headlight/ taillight design", "Appearance of tires/ wheels"]),
    "Interior design & ambience": (r"interior design|ambient|material|workmanship",
                                   ["Overall interior styling/ aesthetics", "Interior lighting",
                                    "Quality of interior materials", "Overall interior workmanship"]),
    "Audio": (r"audio|sound system|speaker",
              ["Overall performance of sound system", "Audio clarity", "Bass performance"]),
    "Noise & quality": (r"noise|rattl|squeak|vibration",
                        ["Overall noise/vibration/harshness", "Freedom from squeaks and rattles",
                         "Freedom from wind and road noise"]),
    "Value & ownership": (r"price|cost|warranty|service|dealer",
                          ["Overall value for money", "Affordable to buy", "Future trade-in or resale value",
                           "Economical to own (cost of ownership)"]),
}

all_topics = cl["topic"].unique()
bev_ids = set(feedbacks.loc[feedbacks.powertrain == "BEV", "ID"])
rows, topic_map = [], {}
for area, (pattern, attrs) in AREAS.items():
    tps = [t for t in all_topics if re.search(pattern, t, re.I)]
    topic_map[area] = tps
    r = cl[cl["topic"].isin(tps)]
    ids_pain = r[r.ftype.isin(["Difficult to Use", "Defect"])]["ID"].unique()
    ids_want = r[r.ftype == "Wants"]["ID"].unique()
    ids_like = r[r.ftype == "Likes"]["ID"].unique()
    attrs = [a for a in attrs if a in s60.index]
    sev = probs[probs["ID"].isin(r["ID"])]
    rows.append({
        "area": area,
        "topics matched": len(tps),
        "pain feedbacks": len(ids_pain),
        "wants feedbacks": len(ids_want),
        "likes feedbacks": len(ids_like),
        "net sentiment": (len(ids_like) - len(ids_pain) - len(ids_want)) / max(1, len(set(r["ID"]))),
        "BEV share of pain": np.mean([i in bev_ids for i in ids_pain]) if len(ids_pain) else np.nan,
        "serious C reports": int(sev["severity"].isin(["serious", "very serious"]).sum()),
        "study attrs": len(attrs),
        "study mean": s60.loc[attrs, "mean"].mean() if attrs else np.nan,
        "study bottom3": s60.loc[attrs, "bottom3"].mean() if attrs else np.nan,
        "top2 vs G70": s60.loc[attrs, "top2_vs_G70"].mean() if attrs else np.nan,
    })
tri = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("area")

# Flag each source: is this area a problem according to it? Thresholds = median across areas.
fb_problem = tri["net sentiment"] < tri["net sentiment"].median()
st_problem = tri["study mean"] < tri["study mean"].median()
tri["agreement"] = np.select(
    [fb_problem & st_problem, ~fb_problem & ~st_problem, fb_problem & ~st_problem],
    ["both: weak", "both: strong", "feedback weak, study fine"], default="study weak, feedback fine")
tri.sort_values("net sentiment").style.format({

md(r"""

## 8. Evidence scorecard: a first, explainable priority order

A deliberately simple, transparent score to seed the PM discussion. It is **not** a final prioritisation. Each
component is turned into a 0–1 percentile rank across the areas, then weighted:

| Component | Weight | Why |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Pain feedbacks (DtU + Defect) | 0.30 | How many customers hit the problem |
| Wants feedbacks | 0.15 | Explicit demand for change |
| Serious / very serious Source C reports | 0.15 | Customer-rated severity |
| Study bottom-3 box | 0.25 | Rejection in a structured survey |
| Gap to G70 (top-2, negative = behind) | 0.15 | Headroom shown by BMW's own flagship |

Strengths with high Likes and good study scores are listed separately as **protect** areas: the successor must not
lose them.
""")

code(r"""
WEIGHTS = {"pain feedbacks": 0.30, "wants feedbacks": 0.15, "serious C reports": 0.15,
           "study bottom3": 0.25, "gap to G70": 0.15}
score_in = tri.assign(**{"gap to G70": -tri["top2 vs G70"]})
pct = score_in[list(WEIGHTS)].rank(pct=True).fillna(0.5)
tri["priority score"] = sum(pct[k] * w for k, w in WEIGHTS.items())
tri["evidence"] = np.where(tri["agreement"] == "both: weak", "converging",
                  np.where(tri["agreement"].str.contains("weak"), "single-source", "—"))

fix = tri.sort_values("priority score", ascending=False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5))
contrib = (pct * pd.Series(WEIGHTS)).loc[fix.index].iloc[::-1]
left = np.zeros(len(contrib))
for k, col in zip(WEIGHTS, ["#e34948", "#6250d6", "#8f1d1c", "#eda100", "#2a78d6"]):

content.text:
I created `notebooks/g60_us_analysis.ipynb` and ran it from start to finish without errors. Before writing the findings in each section, I checked them against the real outputs.

The sales file has only three US numbers for the 5 Series (2024, 2025 and the 2030 forecast). So the notebook covers all the US 5 Series data, with sales as the first section.

**What's in it:**
1. **Sales:** US volume over time, growth by market, and the US share of the 5 Series and of all US sales in the data. It also counts feedbacks per 1,000 cars sold in each market, which shows the US is the only 5 Series market with dense customer feedback (46 per 1k, against about 1 per 1k in Europe and none in China).
2. **Who is giving feedback:** breakdown by channel and engine type, the mix of feedback types, and text length.
3. **Topics:** the most liked topics, the biggest pain points, what customers ask for, the most negative topics, and topics that come up together.
4. **Electric vs petrol/diesel:** EV-only topics (range, charging) against petrol/diesel-leaning ones (auto start-stop, cruise control, touchscreen).
5. **Channel deep dives:** severity-rated problem reports from the quality survey (Source C), the "love most / could be most improved" survey (Source D), and sample customer quotes for the top pain topics.
6. **US customer study:** all 103 attributes, grouped into areas and compared with the 7 Series.
7. **Cross-check:** 18 requirement areas, each mapped by hand to its feedback topics and survey questions. Each one is labelled by whether the feedback and the survey agree it's weak.
8. **Priority scorecard:** a simple weighted score with the weights shown, plus a list of strengths to protect.
9. **Summary.**

**Main results:**
- **Sales:** About 78k cars a year, nearly flat to 2030 (+0.5% a year). Keeping current owners matters more than winning new buyers.
- **Fix first, by the scorecard:**
  1. Controls and screens
  2. Keys, doors and trunk (the hands-free trunk opening is the most disliked topic)
  3. Climate controls
  4. App and connected services
  5. Range and charging, for the electric i5 only
- **Protect:** ride and handling, drivetrain, and exterior design. They score best in both the feedback and the survey.
- **Behind the 7 Series:** rear-seat space and comfort, standard equipment, and interior material quality.

**Things to know:**
- Running the notebook writes three CSVs to `outputs/` (git-ignored), so your app can reuse the results.
- Two of the lowest survey scores are off-road ability and spare-tire readiness. They aren't relevant for this sedan, so the notebook flags them and leaves them out. Pricing scores are also left out, because the brief puts pricing out of scope.
- The scorecard weights are my own choice, and they're easy to change at the top of section 8. The score favours areas with many complaints, so the drivetrain lands mid-table even though it's a strength. That's why strengths are listed separately.
- I haven't committed the notebook. Say if you want it on your branch.

Your mission

Build an AI-powered application that ingests heterogeneous data, derives customer requirements for a vehicle, prioritizes them, and puts a product manager in the loop at the decisions that matter.

Your app should be able to:
•    Ingest the provided data and enrich it with structured knowledge from the web.
•    Extract signals such as recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages and market trends, each linked to its sources.
•    Derive requirements from those findings: clear, actionable, customer-facing and realistic.
•    Prioritize them with a logic you define and can explain.
•    Involve the PM to approve, reject, edit or challenge requirements and their rationale and evidence behind them. 
•    Record everything in an audit trail (is a complete, chronological record of all actions, changes, and access events within a system or data environment).
About the Scope

In scope:
•    Customer requirements on the product: features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services, design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as experienced by the customer, variant and package offering, etc.

Out of scope:
•    Regulatory and homologation requirements (e.g.: safety, emissions, type approval)
•    Technical and engineering requirements (e.g.: component specs, architecture, supplier topics)
•    Pricing, business case and cost calculation (you may use cost or effort as a rough prioritization factor)
Make it yours!
Demonstrate your application at least for one derivative in onbe market but avoid designing it as a one-off: it should be adaptable to other BMW vehicles and markets. The remaining datasets and scenarios are available for optional testing. 
We know the challenge is broad. Focus on the parts where your team can make the strongest contribution. You might go deep on web research and turn external information into usable evidence, or on integrating and interpreting the provided BMW data. You do not need to develop every capability to the same depth. Be creative, but show how your chosen focus connects to the overall path from evidence to a PM decision.

A concept and demonstrable prototype of an AI-powered product requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization, and integrates human review.

A structured sample list of derived product requirements. It should record relevant changes to requirement content, scores, priorities, evidence, and status, including who or what initiated each change, when it occurred, and the documented rationale.

## 6. Deliverables

### 6.1 What to demonstrate (S1)

- **A concept and working prototype** showing how AI supports the identification, formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements, using the provided data and, where relevant, external sources.
- **A representative set of requirements supported by clear evidence and reasoning.** Show how customer feedback, product data, market signals or competitor insights translate into requirements, and explain the factors driving their prioritization.
- **A transparent decision-support experience** that lets PMs review, challenge, modify, approve or reject AI proposals, with evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and key decisions visible and traceable throughout.

### 6.2 Expected deliverables (S2, section 5)

> S2 jumps from section 3 to section 5; its section 4 is empty in the source.

1. **Concept and demonstrable prototype** of an AI-powered product-requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization and integrates human review.
2. **Structured sample list of derived product requirements.** Every requirement needs all of these fields:
   - [ ] Unique identifier
   - [ ] Clear, actionable description
   - [ ] Linked findings and sources
   - [ ] Priority or score
   - [ ] Applied prioritization rationale
   - [ ] Evidence level
   - [ ] Key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties
   - [ ] Current decision status
3. **Clearly defined end-to-end workflow** showing how inputs become proposed and prioritized requirements, **which activities the AI performs autonomously, and where human review is mandatory**.
4. **Demonstrable audit trail** that makes each requirement traceable from its findings and sources through consolidation, scoring, prioritization and human decision-making. It must record changes to requirement **content, scores, priorities, evidence and status**, including **who or what** initiated each change, **when**, and the **documented rationale**.

> Teams choose their own technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic and UX. The deliverables describe capabilities and outcomes, not a prescribed design. They can be one integrated solution or a set of connected concepts, prototypes, models and visualizations. (S2)

## 7. Provided data (S3)

"Provided data (per vehicle)":

| Dataset | What it contains | What it is good for | Our file(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Customer verbatims** | Free-text customer feedback on the current vehicle | Pain points, unmet needs, what customers love and must not lose | `*_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` |
| **Equipment list** | Standard and optional equipment by trim and market | What the car offers today, gaps against competitors | `*_OptionList.PDF` |
| **Sales volumes** | Units by powertrain and region | Where the car sells, which powertrains matter, where it underperforms | `sales_volumes.xlsx` |
| **Customer study** | Customer ratings in various categories | How customers perceive, like/dislike and rate different components of a car | `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` |

Schemas, value distributions and quirks of each file: [`../datasets/`](../datasets/README.md).

## 8. BMW's framing: from findings to one car (S4)

![From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp)

**1 billion findings › 1,000 requirements › one car.**

> **Customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute of a car.**

- **Example findings (raw customer voice):** "Charging takes too long." · "The NEW XPENG." · "Too many menus." · "Ugly kidney grille." · "I love the design." · "Too much plastic." · "More rear space, please." · "Uncomfortable seats." · "The app should just work." · "Very nice exterior colors." · "Tesla and GROK"
- **Example requirement themes (word cloud):** affordable, easy updates, data privacy, safety, joy of driving, flexible storage, everyday space, efficiency, connected, design, great sound, easy charging, reliable software, clear displays, easy entry, seat ventilation, home charging, art app, **intuitive UX**, iconic design, comfortable seats, smooth ride, fast charging, fast app response, sport wheels, real-world range, easy parking, heated seats, long battery life, personalized, carbon roof, simple maintenance, clear navigation, low running costs, dynamic, room for family, sustainable, easy child seat fit, electric, physical controls, **premium feel**, **range**
- Visual: "Future BMW sedan" (AI concept visual).

Takeaway: the job is **condensing many noisy, overlapping findings into a manageable set of customer-relevant attributes**. The findings mix complaints, praise, competitor mentions (XPENG, Tesla, Grok) and trends.

## 9. BMW's requirements process (S5)

![The process](sources/slide-the-process.webp)

Five stages, left to right. The slide marks each box with a **robot icon (AI)** and/or a **person icon (human)**:

| Stage | Box | Content on the slide | AI | Human |
| --- | --- | --- | :---: | :---: |
| **1. Situation analysis** | Baseline | Previous BMW model · BMW portfolio · Sales volume | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Competition | | ✓ | |
| | Customer / public feedback | | ✓ | |
| | Product and global trends | | ✓ | |
| **2. Structure & context** | Classify, cluster, contextualize | "AI standardizes findings, identifies duplicates, groups themes and connects insights" | ✓ | |
| | All potential requirements (0/1) | e.g. BEV powertrain, cooler, seat ventilation, … → **"Implement requirement?"** (binary yes/no) | | |
| **3. Requirements definition** | Specification and quantification | "Define measurable targets and acceptance criteria" | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Metric specification | e.g. *Range: 600 or 700 mi?* · *Cooler: for how many bottles?* · *Seat ventilation: fast enough?* | | |
| | (unlabeled column, likely domains) | Exterior · Interior · Powertrain · Driver assistance · … | | |
| **4. Prioritization** | | Customer · Business · … | ✓ | ✓ |
| **5. Documentation** | Requirements tracking | (cycle icon: continuous tracking) | ✓ | |

Reading of the slide (our interpretation):

- **AI-only (autonomous) steps:** gathering competition, feedback and trends; classifying, clustering and de-duplicating findings; documentation and requirements tracking.
- **AI + human (review mandatory) steps:** setting the baseline, specifying and quantifying requirements, prioritization. These map directly onto deliverable 6.2 #3 ("where human review is mandatory").
- Requirements go through two levels: first a **binary decision** (implement: 0/1), then a **metric specification** (how much / how good).
- Prioritization weighs **customer** value against **business** factors.

## 10. Related inputs from BMW people

- Notes from the conversation with a BMW product manager: [`../bmw-pm-interview/`](../bmw-pm-interview/). It covers the signal channels, the prioritization questions BMW actually asks, the 1–2 year iteration loop, and how lines between vehicle classes are drawn.

## 11. Quick facts

| --- | --- |
| Vehicles (e-codes) | **F70** = 1 Series · **G60** = 5 Series sedan · **G68** = 5 Series long wheelbase (China; customer study only) · **G70** = 7 Series |
| Markets in focus | Europe, China, USA (any subset) |
| Horizon | Successor vehicle, 3–5 years ahead |
| Minimum demo | ≥ 1 derivative in ≥ 1 market, built to generalize |
| Hard constraints | Customer-facing requirements only; no regulatory, engineering or pricing work |
| Must-haves | Requirement list (8 fields), E2E workflow with AI-vs-human split, audit trail, PM-in-the-loop prototype |

## 6. Deliverables

### 6.1 What to demonstrate (S1)

- **A concept and working prototype** showing how AI supports the identification, formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements, using the provided data and, where relevant, external sources.
- **A representative set of requirements supported by clear evidence and reasoning.** Show how customer feedback, product data, market signals or competitor insights translate into requirements, and explain the factors driving their prioritization.
- **A transparent decision-support experience** that lets PMs review, challenge, modify, approve or reject AI proposals, with evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and key decisions visible and traceable throughout.

### 6.2 Expected deliverables (S2, section 5)

> S2 jumps from section 3 to section 5; its section 4 is empty in the source.

1. **Concept and demonstrable prototype** of an AI-powered product-requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization and integrates human review.
2. **Structured sample list of derived product requirements.** Every requirement needs all of these fields:
   - [ ] Unique identifier
   - [ ] Clear, actionable description
   - [ ] Linked findings and sources
   - [ ] Priority or score
   - [ ] Applied prioritization rationale
   - [ ] Evidence level
   - [ ] Key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties
   - [ ] Current decision status
3. **Clearly defined end-to-end workflow** showing how inputs become proposed and prioritized requirements, **which activities the AI performs autonomously, and where human review is mandatory**.
4. **Demonstrable audit trail** that makes each requirement traceable from its findings and sources through consolidation, scoring, prioritization and human decision-making. It must record changes to requirement **content, scores, priorities, evidence and status**, including **who or what** initiated each change, **when**, and the **documented rationale**.

> Teams choose their own technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic and UX. The deliverables describe capabilities and outcomes, not a prescribed design. They can be one integrated solution or a set of connected concepts, prototypes, models and visualizations. (S2)

## 7. Provided data (S3)

"Provided data (per vehicle)":

| Dataset | What it contains | What it is good for | Our file(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Customer verbatims** | Free-text customer feedback on the current vehicle | Pain points, unmet needs, what customers love and must not lose | `*_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` |
| **Equipment list** | Standard and optional equipment by trim and market | What the car offers today, gaps against competitors | `*_OptionList.PDF` |
| **Sales volumes** | Units by powertrain and region | Where the car sells, which powertrains matter, where it underperforms | `sales_volumes.xlsx` |
| **Customer study** | Customer ratings in various categories | How customers perceive, like/dislike and rate different components of a car | `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` |

Schemas, value distributions and quirks of each file: [`../datasets/`](../datasets/README.md).

## 8. BMW's framing: from findings to one car (S4)

![From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp)

**1 billion findings › 1,000 requirements › one car.**

> **Customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute of a car.**

- **Example findings (raw customer voice):** "Charging takes too long." · "The NEW XPENG." · "Too many menus." · "Ugly kidney grille." · "I love the design." · "Too much plastic." · "More rear space, please." · "Uncomfortable seats." · "The app should just work." · "Very nice exterior colors." · "Tesla and GROK"
- **Example requirement themes (word cloud):** affordable, easy updates, data privacy, safety, joy of driving, flexible storage, everyday space, efficiency, connected, design, great sound, easy charging, reliable software, clear displays, easy entry, seat ventilation, home charging, art app, **intuitive UX**, iconic design, comfortable seats, smooth ride, fast charging, fast app response, sport wheels, real-world range, easy parking, heated seats, long battery life, personalized, carbon roof, simple maintenance, clear navigation, low running costs, dynamic, room for family, sustainable, easy child seat fit, electric, physical controls, **premium feel**, **range**
- Visual: "Future BMW sedan" (AI concept visual).

Takeaway: the job is **condensing many noisy, overlapping findings into a manageable set of customer-relevant attributes**. The findings mix complaints, praise, competitor mentions (XPENG, Tesla, Grok) and trends.

## 9. BMW's requirements process (S5)

![The process](sources/slide-the-process.webp)

Five stages, left to right. The slide marks each box with a **robot icon (AI)** and/or a **person icon (human)**:

| Stage | Box | Content on the slide | AI | Human |
| --- | --- | --- | :---: | :---: |
| **1. Situation analysis** | Baseline | Previous BMW model · BMW portfolio · Sales volume | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Competition | | ✓ | |
| | Customer / public feedback | | ✓ | |
| | Product and global trends | | ✓ | |
| **2. Structure & context** | Classify, cluster, contextualize | "AI standardizes findings, identifies duplicates, groups themes and connects insights" | ✓ | |
| | All potential requirements (0/1) | e.g. BEV powertrain, cooler, seat ventilation, … → **"Implement requirement?"** (binary yes/no) | | |
| **3. Requirements definition** | Specification and quantification | "Define measurable targets and acceptance criteria" | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Metric specification | e.g. *Range: 600 or 700 mi?* · *Cooler: for how many bottles?* · *Seat ventilation: fast enough?* | | |
| | (unlabeled column, likely domains) | Exterior · Interior · Powertrain · Driver assistance · … | | |
| **4. Prioritization** | | Customer · Business · … | ✓ | ✓ |
| **5. Documentation** | Requirements tracking | (cycle icon: continuous tracking) | ✓ | |

Reading of the slide (our interpretation):

- **AI-only (autonomous) steps:** gathering competition, feedback and trends; classifying, clustering and de-duplicating findings; documentation and requirements tracking.
- **AI + human (review mandatory) steps:** setting the baseline, specifying and quantifying requirements, prioritization. These map directly onto deliverable 6.2 #3 ("where human review is mandatory").
- Requirements go through two levels: first a **binary decision** (implement: 0/1), then a **metric specification** (how much / how good).
- Prioritization weighs **customer** value against **business** factors.

## 10. Related inputs from BMW people

- Notes from the conversation with a BMW product manager: [`../bmw-pm-interview/`](../bmw-pm-interview/). It covers the signal channels, the prioritization questions BMW actually asks, the 1–2 year iteration loop, and how lines between vehicle classes are drawn.

Partly. `docs/challenge/brief.md` already has most of the pasted challenge text, but not the newer additions.

**Already in `brief.md`:**
- **Mission and the six capabilities** (ingest, extract signals, derive, prioritize, PM review, audit trail) are in §3.2.
- **In and out of scope** is in §4, including "cost or effort may be used as a rough prioritization factor".
- **"Make it yours"** (at least one derivative in one market, built to adapt to others) is in §5.
- **The four deliverables**, including the 8 fields each requirement needs, are in §6.2.

**Not in `brief.md`:**
1. **Evaluation criteria (your screenshot).** The five judging criteria are not in the file:
   - Decision and Scoring Logic
   - Workflow and Human Decision-Making
   - Traceability and Auditability
   - Solution Quality, Usability and Feasibility
   - Innovation, Scalability and Business Impact
2. **"We reward honesty."** The brief mentions uncertainty and conflicting evidence briefly (§5, "What BMW values"), but not the explicit point that showing where evidence is missing or conflicting counts as a strength.
3. **PM pain points (the answer to the question you received):**
   - Balancing requirements across markets, since climate, how customers use the car and culture differ.
   - Getting early customer feedback, for example on the previous model, and turning it into future requirements.
4. **The roughly two-year process.** The 1–2 year loop appears only in the PM interview notes (`docs/bmw-pm-interview/`), which the brief points to in §10. It isn't stated as part of the official challenge context.
5. **BMW Annual Report tip.** Not mentioned anywhere in `docs/`. It suggests using two areas: market and sales data (regional trends, series deliveries, EV adoption) and product strategy and R&D (ConnectedDrive and My BMW App figures, the Neue Klasse platform).

**Why this matters for your US 5 Series work:**
- The notebook already covers several criteria. The scorecard shows its weights, which fits Decision and Scoring Logic. The evidence labels flag areas with no survey data or only one source, which fits the honesty point. Every area links back to its feedback IDs, which fits traceability.
- The cross-market pain point is a fair challenge to focusing on one market. The answer is that the US is the main demo, built so other markets can be added. Notebook section 1.2 shows Europe and China have almost no feedback for the 5 Series, so you can say this openly as a limitation.
- The two-year process means requirements need a status and a history over time, not just a final list. That supports making the audit trail central.

Should I add a new section to `brief.md` with the evaluation criteria, the honesty point, the PM pain points, the two-year loop and the Annual Report tip, each marked with its source?

p='docs/challenge/brief.md'; s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('''| S5 | [`slide-the-process.webp`](sources/slide-the-process.webp) | Slide "The process" (BMW's requirements workflow) |
''','''| S5 | [`slide-the-process.webp`](sources/slide-the-process.webp) | Slide "The process" (BMW's requirements workflow) |
| S6 | [`slide-evaluation-criteria.png`](sources/slide-evaluation-criteria.png) | Table "Evaluation criteria" (how BMW judges submissions) |
| S7 | BMW answer to a participant question (shared during the event, pasted by the team) | Common PM pain points; the requirement process runs about two years |
| S8 | BMW hint on the BMW Annual Report (shared during the event, pasted by the team) | Which parts of the Annual Report to use as evidence |
''',1)
s=s.rstrip('\n')+'''
| Judged on | Scoring logic, workflow & human decisions, traceability, solution quality, innovation & scale ([§ 12](#12-evaluation-criteria-s6)); honesty about uncertainty is rewarded |

## 12. Evaluation criteria (S6)

| Criterion | What BMW looks for |
| --- | --- |
| **Decision and scoring logic** | Quality, consistency and explainability of the method used to derive, evaluate, score and prioritize requirements. Show **which factors influence decisions**, **how evidence and data sources are weighted and combined**, and **how trade-offs, uncertainties and conflicting signals are resolved**. |
| **Workflow and human decision-making** | Quality and completeness of the end-to-end workflow from heterogeneous findings to prioritized requirements, with clearly defined **roles, decision gates, review steps**, and boundaries between AI-supported, autonomous and human decisions. |
| **Traceability and auditability** | Every requirement, score, modification and decision can be traced back to its originating evidence and sources, with a **complete, reconstructable history of approvals, modifications, postponements and rejections**. |
| **Solution quality, usability and feasibility** | Quality of the concept or prototype, **usefulness of the generated requirements**, ease of use for PMs and engineering teams, and realistic applicability in a complex enterprise product-development environment. |
| **Innovation, scalability and business impact** | Originality and effectiveness; potential to **scale across products, markets and data volumes**; expected contribution to reducing manual effort and rework, shortening decision cycles and improving requirement and decision quality. |

> **"We reward honesty."** Trustworthy AI acknowledges uncertainty. Show where the app **lacks evidence, encounters conflicting signals or reaches uncertain conclusions**, and how this is surfaced to the PM. Honest limitations are a strength, not a weakness. (S6)

Note: the criteria name **postponements** explicitly, so "postponed" needs to be a decision status next to approved, modified and rejected.

## 13. PM pain points and the process timeline (S7)

BMW's answer when asked what common pain points of product managers are:

1. **Balancing customer requirements across markets and regions.** Preferences differ, for example because of climate, how customers use the car, or culture. The same requirement can matter a lot in one market and little in another.
2. **Accessing early customer feedback and extracting future requirements from it**, for example feedback on predecessor vehicles. The task is to get from today's feedback to what customers will want in the successor.

**The requirement process is not a one-off.** It does not end in a single requirement list. It runs over **about two years**, during which the most relevant requirements are prioritized again and again. This matches the 1–2 year loop in the [PM interview notes](../bmw-pm-interview/).

What this implies for our solution (our reading):

- Requirements need a **lifecycle** (status, versions, re-scoring when new evidence arrives), not just a final list. The audit trail is the backbone of that.
- Market should be a **dimension of every requirement and score**, even if the demo covers one market, so cross-market differences become visible instead of averaged away.

## 14. Extra source hint: BMW Annual Report (S8)

BMW suggests the **BMW Annual Report** as backing evidence. There is no need to read the financial breakdown; focus on two areas:

| Area | What to extract | Use in our app |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Market and sales data** | Regional growth trends, deliveries by model series (e.g. X models vs sedans), latest EV adoption rates | Target persona, proof of market demand, where a requirement has the biggest impact |
| **Product strategy and R&D** | R&D investment priorities, ConnectedDrive and My BMW App metrics, the **Neue Klasse** platform strategy | Showing that a requirement is feasible and aligned with BMW's current investments and future vehicle architecture |

The Annual Report is not in `data/` yet. Whatever we use from it should be cited like any other source (document, year, page).
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
r='docs/README.md'; t=open(r).read()

''','''| Where does BMW expect AI vs human review? | [brief.md § 9 Process](challenge/brief.md#9-bmws-requirements-process-s5) |
| How will we be judged? | [brief.md § 12 Evaluation criteria](challenge/brief.md#12-evaluation-criteria-s6) |
| What are PMs' real pain points? | [brief.md § 13](challenge/brief.md#13-pm-pain-points-and-the-process-timeline-s7) |
''',1)
open(r,'w').write(t)
EOF

+## 12. Evaluation criteria (S6)
+| Criterion | What BMW looks for |

+| **Decision and scoring logic** | Quality, consistency and explainability of the method used to derive, evaluate, score and prioritize requirements. Show **which factors influence decisions**, **how evidence and data sources are weighted and combined**, and **how trade-offs, uncertainties and conflicting signals are resolved**. |

+| **Traceability and auditability** | Every requirement, score, modification and decision can be traced back to its originating evidence and sources, with a **complete, reconstructable history of approvals, modifications, postponements and rejections**. |

+| **Solution quality, usability and feasibility** | Quality of the concept or prototype, **usefulness of the generated requirements**, ease of use for PMs and engineering teams, and realistic applicability in a complex enterprise product-development environment. |

+2. **Accessing early customer feedback and extracting future requirements from it**, for example feedback on predecessor vehicles. The task is to get from today's feedback to what customers will want in the successor.
